analysis.one_liner: Turns the 2001 Roadless Rule into law, banning new road construction and logging in inventoried roadless national forest areas.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 21 Senate cosponsors all Democrats or Independents, was referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write the 2001 Roadless Rule into federal law, permanently barring the Forest Service from allowing new roads, rebuilt roads, or commercial logging in designated roadless areas of the national forests. Those areas supply drinking water to tens of millions of Americans, support recreation-based local economies, and provide hunting, fishing, and backcountry access. The bill leaves existing roads, existing access, and all uses outside roadless areas untouched. It was referred to committee in March 2021 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who hunt, fish, hike, camp, or bike in national forest backcountry, the tens of millions of Americans whose drinking water originates in healthy roadless watersheds, and small communities with recreation-based economies that depend on unroaded public land. Downstream water users also benefit because undisturbed watersheds filter water for free, saving communities millions of dollars in treatment costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hunters, anglers, recreation towns, and water users

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars the Forest Service from allowing road construction, road reconstruction, or logging in inventoried roadless areas where the Roadless Rule prohibits those activities, giving a regulation that can be changed by any future administration the force of statute.

The bill's findings state that roadless watersheds provide drinking water to tens of millions of Americans and that keeping roadless areas undisturbed saves downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs.

The bill's findings note that roadless areas support hunting, fishing, hiking, camping, skiing, and mountain biking, allow many mechanized uses that wilderness areas forbid, and underpin recreation-based local economies that depend on public land without roads for jobs, revenue, and consumer spending.
The findings also cite the Forest Service's 371,581-mile existing road system with a $3.2 billion maintenance backlog, arguing that adding new roads compounds a cost taxpayers already cannot cover.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry, which would lose any future chance to log inventoried roadless areas, and road-building and timber-support contractors who work on national forest road projects. Rural counties that receive a share of federal timber revenue, and off-road users who might want new access routes into roadless country, would also forgo those uses. Fire-management agencies lose one potential tool, since the bill's own findings note fires are rarer but harder to fight in roadless areas once started.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently locks in a regulatory decision made in 2001, removing the ability of future administrations or local forest managers to open specific roadless areas to logging even if conditions change, and critics have long argued the Roadless Rule leaves western forests more vulnerable to catastrophic wildfire and insect damage by restricting mechanical thinning.

The bill's own text acknowledges that wildfires are almost twice as likely in roaded areas but harder to access in roadless areas, so the logging ban means some fires will be fought with less road access and higher suppression costs.
Rural communities and counties that historically counted on timber harvests and forest road work for jobs and revenue would have no path to recover those uses on roadless land.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most ordinary people the bill's benefits are broad and diffuse: protected drinking water, free natural water filtration, and continued backcountry access for recreation. The costs fall on a much smaller, concentrated group (the timber industry and forest-road contractors) and on residents of fire-prone areas where road access matters for suppression. The strongest objection is that the ban is permanent and inflexible, even for areas where thinning might reduce fire risk; the bill's answer, in its findings, is that fuel-reduction work is still prioritized where it does the most good and that roadless areas are already burned less often than roaded ones.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in March 2021, and sat there with no hearing or vote until Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on March 22, 2021, with 20 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats or the chamber's Independent, Bernie Sanders.
On the day it was introduced, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action appears in the bill's history: it received no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll-call vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber and forest-road-construction interests are better off, since no law now stands in the way of future administrations rolling back the Roadless Rule by regulation, leaving roadless areas open to logging and road building at any time. The Forest Service also avoids having its management discretion narrowed by statute.

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 20 Senate cosponsors, all from her own caucus or the chamber's Independent.

for.name: 19 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to give it initial support.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the remainder of the Congress without scheduling a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Timber and forest products industry
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed statutory codification of the Roadless Rule, which bars logging and road construction on inventoried roadless national forest land.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached the floor for a vote, where its fate likely rested with the Republican minority and the committee's leadership.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar logging in inventoried roadless areas, ending the industry's prospect of harvesting timber there. Its interest in opening those lands runs against the public's interest in watershed protection and backcountry recreation.

The bill bans new road construction and reconstruction in roadless areas, removing a source of federal road-building work. The bill's findings counter that taxpayers face a $3.2 billion backlog on existing roads, so new road spending in roadless areas competes with obligations the public already owes.

Outfitters, guide services, and recreation-dependent towns gain certainty that the backcountry their customers use will stay unroaded. The bill's findings explicitly credit roadless protection with supporting recreation-based economies' jobs and revenue.

industries.industry: Municipal water utilities and downstream water users
industries.note: Undisturbed roadless watersheds filter drinking water naturally; the bill's findings say this saves downstream communities millions of dollars in filtration costs.
